prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The motivation is compelling. In real e-commerce systems, attribute inventories are incomplete, dynamic, and expensive to maintain manually, so a setting that both expands known attribute types and discovers previously unseen ones is valuable. The paper also contributes a new dataset and a method, Amacer, that combines seed supervision with self-supervised and unsupervised regularization. Overall, I found the paper interesting, reasonably well-motivated, and empirically promising, though there are also several methodological and evaluation issues that limit how strongly I can endorse the claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the task formulation. The distinction from closed-world tagging and from zero-shot extraction with explicitly named target attributes is clear and meaningful. The proposed setting is closer to what many industrial pipelines actually need: start from a small curated seed inventory, expand it, and surface new attribute clusters without requiring exhaustive annotation or predefined schemas. This is a worthwhile contribution in itself, especially because the paper explicitly frames evaluation as clustering rather than classification over a fixed ontology. I also appreciate that the authors discuss the practical tradeoff between annotation cost and supervision quality, rather than assuming either fully supervised labels or purely noisy distant supervision.

The dataset contribution also appears useful. WoaM includes both titles and bullet points, which is a meaningful improvement over title-only settings, and the statistics suggest that bullet points indeed contain more unseen types and values. The hybrid seed construction process is sensible: bootstrap from existing product profiles, sanitize heuristically, then apply lightweight human curation. This is more realistic than assuming clean labels are freely available. The paper is also commendably transparent that the test set includes many unseen values and a substantial fraction of unseen types. If the released data and code are complete and reproducible, this could become a valuable benchmark for lightly supervised open-world extraction.

Methodologically, the paper is strongest when it stays simple. The syntax-based candidate generation via POS patterns is straightforward, scalable, and apparently effective. The adaptive expansion stage for known seed attributes is also intuitive and well aligned with the task. The empirical comparison against segmentation-based candidate generation is convincing enough to suggest that this design choice matters. Likewise, replacing more cumbersome triplet/regression objectives with a supervised contrastive loss is a reasonable simplification.

The more novel part is the use of implicit signals for new attribute discovery: a bullet-point-level self-supervised contrastive heuristic and a latent-attribute neural topic-model-style regularizer. This is an interesting idea. The intuition that product context contains weak semantic structure beyond the seed set is plausible, and the reported gains over the seed-only variant suggest that these signals help. In particular, the decomposition showing larger gains on new attributes than on seed attributes supports the paper’s central claim that the regularization is especially useful for unseen types.

That said, I have several concerns about the rigor of the experimental validation and about some aspects of the formulation.

My main concern is evaluation. The paper defines a “pseudo precision” as the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI, and then computes a pseudo-F1 with recall. This is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different scales and behaviors; averaging them and treating the result as precision is not theoretically justified. As a result, the headline F1 improvements are difficult to map to standard notions of extraction quality. The paper does provide span-level precision/recall/F1 separately in Table 5, which is helpful, but the main conclusions rely heavily on the pseudo-F1. I would have liked a clearer primary metric grounded in either cluster-level B-cubed / CEAF-style measures, pairwise precision/recall, or a more standard open information extraction clustering evaluation. At minimum, the paper should justify why averaging these three metrics is meaningful and show that conclusions are robust under alternative evaluation protocols.

Relatedly, the clustering evaluation seems to conflate two subproblems: candidate span extraction and attribute grouping. The paper partially addresses this by evaluating with gold spans as candidates, which is good, but the main reported numbers still mix extraction and clustering quality. Since the candidate generation stage is a major component and also a major source of noise, it would be useful to more systematically separate: candidate recall, candidate precision, clustering quality on matched candidates, and end-to-end quality. Table 5 helps, but more decomposition would strengthen the claims.

A second concern is fairness and strength of baselines. The paper compares against closed-world tagging models, OA-Mine, and several internal ablations. However, the strongest comparisons are mostly against OA-Mine variants adapted to the new candidate generation. Because the task setting and dataset differ from prior work, some baseline weakness is expected, but the paper would be stronger with more competitive modern baselines for representation learning and clustering. For example, one could compare against sentence-transformer embeddings with simple clustering, prompt-based embedding models, or stronger unsupervised phrase mining / noun phrase extraction pipelines. The current DBSCAN and OA-Mine baselines may not fully establish that the gains come from the proposed implicit-signal formulation rather than from better candidate generation and cleaner seeds.

A third concern is that the candidate generation strategy, while effective, may encode a substantial amount of hidden supervision from product profiles. The POS patterns are derived from profile attribute values, which are themselves a structured resource. This is not necessarily a problem, but the paper sometimes presents the candidate generation as largely syntax-based and supervision-light. In reality, the pattern inventory is induced from attribute values, so it is a form of weak supervision. I would encourage the authors to be more explicit about this and to quantify how much performance depends on this source. For example, how well would generic noun phrase extraction or manually chosen POS templates perform? How category-specific are the induced patterns? Does cross-category transfer work?

There are also some technical questions about the latent attribute model. The formulation is inspired by neural topic models, but the connection between latent topics and attribute clusters is only partial. Products often contain multiple mentions of the same attribute type and many non-attribute spans; moreover, the bag-of-spans assumption may be quite coarse. The paper acknowledges topic collapse qualitatively, but does not analyze its impact quantitatively. Since the latent attribute module is one of the paper’s main novelties, I would have liked more ablations: self-supervised loss only, latent-attribute loss only, varying K, sensitivity to lambda values, and perhaps diagnostics on learned latent attributes beyond a few cherry-picked examples. The statement that the latent attribute formulation contributes around 70% of the regularization improvement is interesting, but the paper should present the exact ablation table prominently rather than only summarizing it in text.

Another issue is the limited scale and diversity of the dataset. Four categories and roughly 36 seed types overall are a reasonable start, but still narrow for claims about “open-world product attribute mining” broadly. The categories are also all from Amazon and all in English. Since the method depends on POS tagging quality and category-specific product profile resources, its generality remains uncertain. This does not invalidate the contribution, but the claims should be calibrated more carefully. The paper is strongest as a benchmark and method for lightly supervised open-world attribute mining in a constrained e-commerce setting, not yet as a general solution.

I also have some concerns about annotation and ontology ambiguity. The paper says annotators label all spans that are “reasonable attribute values” and assign each span a single best attribute type, with no overlapping spans. In open-world settings, this is inherently subjective. For example, some spans could plausibly belong to multiple types or to different granularities. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedures, or examples of difficult cases beyond a few qualitative illustrations. Since evaluation depends heavily on clustering against these labels, annotation reliability is important. This is especially true for new attribute types, where type boundaries may be fuzzy. Reporting agreement on span boundaries and type assignments would substantially strengthen the dataset contribution.

The paper’s statistical significance claims are also somewhat underdeveloped. It mentions t-tests with >95% confidence, but it is unclear what the sample units are. If the macro-average is over only four product categories, a t-test is not very meaningful. If the units are products or sequences, independence assumptions may be questionable. The paper should clarify the significance testing protocol.

On the positive side, the analysis sections are useful. The decomposition by seed vs new types and title vs bullet points is informative, and the gold-span evaluation is a good diagnostic. The qualitative examples are also honest: they show both successful seed expansion and failure modes where new attributes are absorbed into existing ones. This supports the paper’s claim that open-world discovery remains difficult. I also appreciate the discussion of limitations, though it could go further in acknowledging dependence on English POS tagging and on profile-derived resources.

A few more specific comments and questions:

The adaptive expansion threshold is based on average intra-seed cosine distance. This is intuitive, but it may be unstable for attributes with very small or semantically diverse seed sets. Some analysis by seed set size or attribute heterogeneity would be useful.

The self-supervised heuristic assumes spans in the same bullet point are semantically related and spans in different bullet points of the same product are less related. This is plausible but noisy. It would help to quantify how often bullet points contain multiple unrelated attributes or how sensitive the method is to this assumption.

The candidate generation removes overlapping spans by prioritizing longer spans. This may hurt extraction of nested attributes or compositional values. Since the annotation also disallows overlap, this is consistent with evaluation, but it may artificially simplify the problem.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes “discovering values from 39% new types.” This is an interesting statistic, but it is weaker than discovering 39% of new values or achieving high recall on new types. It would help to define this metric precisely and contextualize it with absolute counts and per-category breakdowns.

The comparison to closed-world tagging models is somewhat expected to favor open-world methods because the evaluation rewards discovery of unseen types. These baselines are useful for context but should not be overinterpreted.

In terms of writing, the paper is generally understandable, but there are many grammatical issues and awkward phrasings throughout. These do not obscure the main ideas, but they do reduce polish. A careful language revision would improve readability. Some notation could also be tightened; for example, the supervised contrastive denominator appears to exclude positives in a way that differs from standard formulations, and the KL term notation in the latent model is a bit imprecise.

Overall, I think this is a meaningful paper with a good problem formulation, a potentially useful dataset, and a method that combines practical engineering choices with some novel weakly supervised regularization ideas. The empirical gains are encouraging, especially on new attribute discovery. However, the evaluation methodology is unconventional, the baseline suite could be stronger, and the evidence for the latent attribute component is not yet as rigorous as I would like for a top-tier venue. I would lean positive if the venue values practical new task formulations and benchmark creation, but I would want the authors to substantially strengthen the evaluation justification, annotation reliability reporting, and ablation analysis.

My recommendation is borderline positive. The paper has clear merit and likely impact, but also notable weaknesses in rigor that should be addressed in revision.

To improve the paper, I would most strongly suggest the following. First, replace or supplement the pseudo-F1 with more standard clustering/extraction metrics and show that the main conclusions hold. Second, report annotation agreement and more details on adjudication for the test set. Third, provide fuller ablations isolating candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning, self-supervised regularization, and latent attributes, including sensitivity analyses. Fourth, strengthen baselines with more modern embedding and clustering alternatives. Fifth, clarify the extent to which profile-derived POS patterns constitute supervision and analyze transferability across categories. If these issues are addressed, the work would be considerably stronger.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where a model must both expand values for known seed attribute types and discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicit type descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset from four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for discovering additional clusters, and two weak regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised within-bullet contrastive objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their proposed clustering-based evaluation, with especially notable gains on new attribute types and bullet-point descriptions.
strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction: discovering unseen attribute types under limited supervision.
Introduces a new dataset with richer product context than prior title-only datasets, including bullet points and a substantial proportion of unseen attribute types and values.
The overall system design is intuitive and modular: candidate generation, representation learning, seed expansion, and new-cluster discovery are clearly separated.
The use of curated seed attributes rather than noisy distant supervision is a meaningful practical contribution.
Empirical gains over adapted baselines are reasonably large on the proposed benchmark, and the paper includes useful ablations such as removing regularization and using gold spans.
The analysis decomposes performance by seed vs. new types and title vs. bullet points, which helps clarify where gains come from.
The paper is generally transparent about limitations, including noisy candidate spans and topic collapse in latent attributes.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret: the main F1 is derived from averaging Jaccard/ARI/NMI as a pseudo-precision and combining it with recall, which lacks a standard theoretical justification.

The proposed supervised contrastive loss appears to be incorrectly formulated: the denominator excludes positives and possibly the anchor itself, differing from standard supervised contrastive learning and making the objective mathematically questionable.

The latent-attribute model is only loosely connected to attribute discovery quality; its formulation and optimization details are underspecified, and the empirical gains from it are modest in absolute terms.

Candidate generation relies heavily on POS patterns extracted from product profiles, which may leak domain-specific structure from auxiliary resources and may not generalize beyond English or beyond categories with similar profile quality.

Comparisons to baselines are not fully balanced because several baselines are adapted to the authors' candidate generation or setting, while the proposed method benefits from multiple pipeline changes simultaneously.
The benchmark covers only four categories, so claims about open-world generality are limited.
The paper lacks annotation quality statistics for the human-labeled test set (e.g., inter-annotator agreement), which is important given the subjectivity of span boundaries and new attribute types.
Statistical significance claims are weakly documented; a t-test over only four categories is not very convincing.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive objective in Eq. for L_su is not the standard supervised contrastive loss. In standard formulations, the denominator includes all non-anchor examples (including positives), whereas here it sums only over negatives. This changes the optimization behavior substantially and may make the probabilistic interpretation invalid. The same issue appears in the self-supervised contrastive loss L_ss.

The paper defines cosine as a distance in Section 5, but cosine similarity is used elsewhere as a similarity score. In Eq. (1)-(2), averaging 'cosine distance' while thresholding by average within-support 'cosine' is ambiguous and potentially inconsistent unless carefully defined; this affects reproducibility and scientific clarity.

The main evaluation metric ('pseudo-F1') is ad hoc: averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI to form a pseudo-precision and then combining with recall is not a validated clustering metric. Because these quantities have different statistical meanings and scales, improvements in the reported F1 may not correspond to better attribute mining quality in a principled sense.

The latent-attribute ELBO description is mathematically imprecise. The KL term is written as KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}), but \tilde{\alpha}^p is sampled Gaussian logits before softmax while \hat{\alpha} is described as a standard Gaussian prior Product-to-Attribute distribution; the notation conflates Gaussian latent variables with simplex-valued attribute probabilities.

The self-supervised heuristic assumes spans in the same bullet point are semantically related and spans in different bullet points of the same product are negatives. This can be systematically false in product descriptions where one bullet contains multiple unrelated attributes and multiple bullets discuss the same attribute, potentially injecting contradictory supervision.

Empirical validity is limited by low span extraction quality: Table 5 shows exact span F1 below 37 and precision below 34. Since clustering is evaluated only on predicted/gold span matches, much of the end-task difficulty may stem from candidate generation rather than attribute modeling, and the paper's conclusions about open-world attribute discovery are therefore somewhat confounded.

The significance test is not reliable with such a small number of macro-averaged units (apparently four categories). Without multiple random seeds and variance across runs, it is difficult to assess robustness of the reported gains.
